questions.question: Define a closure precisely. Why does it depend on lexical scope, and when is the captured environment created?
questions.answer:
A closure is a function together with the lexical environment in which it was created. That environment is a record of the variables in scope at the definition site, and the function keeps a live reference to it, so the variables stay reachable even after the outer function returns. This is why a function returned from makeGreeter('Hi') can still read greeting.

It depends on lexical scope because JavaScript resolves names by where code is written, not by who calls it. The engine walks the scope chain of the definition site — inner function, then enclosing function, then module, then global. Each call of the outer function creates a fresh environment, so two calls produce two independent closures; that is what makes per-instance counters work. A closure is created whenever a function is created, but it only becomes observable when the inner function outlives its outer scope or is passed somewhere that calls it later.
key_points: Closure = function + its lexical environment
Names resolve where the function was written, not where it is called
Each outer call creates a fresh environment → independent state
Observable when the inner function outlives the outer scope

Output: var 3, var 3, var 3, let 0, let 1, let 2.

var is function-scoped, so the loop has exactly one binding of i, shared by all three callbacks. The timers run after the loop finishes, by which time i is 3. let is block-scoped and the for loop creates a new binding per iteration (copied from the previous one), so each callback closes over its own j.

Pre-let fixes: wrap the body in an IIFE — ((n) => setTimeout(() => console.log(n), 0))(i) — or use forEach over an array, whose callback already receives a per-item parameter. The bug is not about setTimeout; any deferred callback (event listener, promise, interval) shows it.
key_points: var = one shared function-scoped binding for the whole loop
let = a fresh binding per iteration
Timers run after the loop, so they see the final value
Fixes: let, an IIFE, or forEach's per-item parameter

questions.question: How does a closure provide private state, and how does the module pattern use that? Compare it with class private fields.
questions.answer:
A closure gives privacy because the variable is not a property of the returned object — it exists only in the environment captured by the functions you expose. Callers can invoke those functions but cannot read or assign the variable directly; there is no key to enumerate, no JSON serialization, no accidental external write. The module pattern wraps this in an IIFE: it creates the state and returns an object with only the public methods, so the object is the API and the closure is the hidden implementation.

A class private field (#count) gives the same external inaccessibility with class syntax and per-instance storage, and the engine enforces it (accessing obj.#count outside the class is a syntax error). Closure privacy is enforced by scope, which also means it works without classes and can hide multiple variables and helper functions. The trade-offs: closures cost one function object per method per instance unless methods are defined on the returned object once, and private fields are not accessible to subclasses, whereas closure state is simply invisible to everyone.
key_points: Private = captured variable, not an object property
Module pattern: IIFE creates state, returns a public API
Class #fields give the same privacy with class syntax
Closure privacy is scope-based; #fields are engine-enforced

questions.answer:
It prints 5, then 'Kakade'.

The first part proves that a closure captures the **variable binding**, not a snapshot of its value at definition time. `get` closes over n, and n is reassigned to 5 before the function is returned, so get() sees 5. If you need the value at definition time, copy it into a new const inside a scope: const snapshot = n; return () => snapshot.

The second part shows that a closure does not capture this by itself — an arrow function inherits this from the enclosing scope, which is the greet method, whose this is user. With a normal function inside greet, this would be undefined in strict/module code and the call would throw. This is why arrows are the standard fix for `this` inside callbacks.
key_points: Closures capture the binding, not the value at creation time
Later reassignment is visible through the closure
Copy into a const to snapshot a value
Arrows inherit this lexically; normal functions get their own

questions.question: How do closures cause memory leaks, and what are the practical ways to avoid them?
questions.answer:
A closure keeps its captured environment alive for as long as the function object is reachable. If that function is stored somewhere long-lived — an event listener on window, a setInterval callback, a global cache, a subscription — then everything it references stays alive too, even if the rest of the app no longer needs it. A single returned function that reads one field can pin a large object, because the environment is retained as a unit (engines optimise to the variables actually referenced, but that is an implementation detail, not a guarantee).

Practical fixes: remove listeners with removeEventListener or an AbortSignal; clear intervals and timeouts on teardown; bound caches (LRU or a max size) instead of letting a Map grow forever; capture only the value you need (const id = big.id) instead of the whole object; and use WeakMap/WeakSet when attaching data to objects you do not own, so entries disappear when the key is collected. In browsers, detached DOM nodes retained by a closure are a very common leak — the Heap snapshot showing 'Detached' nodes is the tell.
key_points: Closures retain captured environments while reachable
Long-lived listeners, timers and caches are the usual culprits
Remove listeners, clear timers, bound caches
WeakMap/WeakSet allow garbage collection of keys
Detached DOM nodes retained by handlers are a classic browser leak
